lesson.title: Mercantilism: The Economic Logic Behind Empire
lesson.summary: Mercantilism, the dominant economic theory of early modern Europe, held that colonies existed to enrich the mother country by supplying raw materials and buying finished goods, a philosophy that shaped England's entire approach to its American possessions.
lesson.body:
Mercantilism was the economic philosophy that guided most European powers, including England, from roughly the sixteenth through the eighteenth centuries. Its core assumption was that the world's wealth was essentially fixed, measured above all in gold and silver bullion, so one nation could only grow richer at another nation's expense. Under this zero sum view of the global economy, a country's central goal should be achieving a favorable balance of trade, exporting more in value than it imported, so that precious metals flowed steadily inward rather than outward.

Colonies fit into this system as tools for strengthening the mother country rather than as independent economic actors pursuing their own interests. England viewed its American colonies as sources of raw materials it could not produce at home, tobacco, timber, furs, and later sugar and rice from the Southern Colonies, and as captive markets for English manufactured goods, since colonists were expected to buy finished products from England rather than developing competing industries themselves. This arrangement, in theory, kept money circulating within the empire and out of the hands of rival powers like France, Spain, and the Netherlands, while also making England less dependent on those same rivals for goods it might otherwise have to import from outside its own trading network.

The economic activity already flourishing across the Atlantic, including the triangular trade that moved enslaved Africans, raw materials, and manufactured goods among Europe, Africa, and the Americas, fit naturally into mercantilist thinking, since it kept valuable commodities and profits flowing through English hands and English ships. Mercantilist theory treated enslaved labor and plantation agriculture as engines for producing exactly the kind of raw materials, sugar, tobacco, indigo, that a mercantilist empire prized most, since they could be sold abroad for hard currency or exchanged for goods England otherwise had to buy from competitors.

To make mercantilist theory work in practice, England needed to control where and how colonial goods were bought and sold, since the whole system depended on colonial trade flowing through English hands rather than leaking away to foreign competitors. This need for control led directly to a series of laws regulating colonial commerce, restricting colonists to shipping certain goods only to England or other English colonies and requiring that trade move on English or colonial built ships. Mercantilism therefore was not merely an abstract economic theory but the intellectual foundation for concrete policy, one that would increasingly put England's interests in direct tension with the economic interests of its American colonists as the decades passed.

Because mercantilist thinking treated colonial prosperity as valuable only insofar as it served the empire as a whole, it left little room for colonists who wanted to trade freely with whichever buyers offered the best price, whether those buyers were English or not. That underlying tension, between an imperial policy designed in London and the practical economic interests of merchants and planters an ocean away, would shape English colonial policy for the rest of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
